transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-07-21
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Luis (Redwood SE), Alex (CTO Novaforge), Maya (ML), Samir (Infra), Tasha (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Walkthrough of Redwood Optimize console focusing on prefetch/prefix KV cache recommendations and batching settings for Novaforge's low-latency conversational workflow.
- Discussed tradeoffs: latency SLO vs token/unit cost, cache hit strategies, sessionization, and when dedicated capacity matters.
- Agreed next steps: share cost model spreadsheet, run throughput sim with sample traces, schedule POC bench.

Topics detected: console demo, prefetch/prefix cache, batching window, concurrency and cold-starts, SOC2/data residency, cost modeling

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: ok hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood Inference, we have Priya and Luis here from the SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:09] Alex: good thanks, Alex here, sorry joining a bit late, got pulled into another sync.
[00:12] Maya: hey, Maya, ML. excited to see the optimize console.
[00:16] Priya: sweet, quick agenda, we'll run through a console demo focused on prefetch/prefix-KV cache and batching recommendations, then then sim a couple cost scenarios with your traffic profile, and leave time for Q and A.
[00:30] Samir: sounds good. main thing for us is meeting 75 ms p95 latency for chat completions, and keeping monthly inference spend under our budget — roughly $25k.
[00:40] Jordan: perfect, we'll keep that in mind. i want to flag up-front that some of the words in the console are auto-labeled as "prefix" vs "prefetch" interchangeably, so we'll call out both.
[00:51] Priya: jumping into the console now — share screen — ok, this is the Optimize console, baseline view shows sample model profiles and a recommendations tab. For Novaforge's conversational workload we typically recommend a hybrid of prefix (lookahead) caching and modest batching.
[01:10] Alex: can you define prefix vs prefetch quickly? we use "session cache" in-house so curious about the difference.
[01:15] Priya: yeah, sure. prefix caching stores KV cache entries for common leading tokens (prompts, system messages) so subsequent calls with the same prefix skip the initial compute. prefetch (console calls it lookahead/prefetch) is proactively warming the KV cache for likely next-turns. both reduce per-token compute but prefetch can increase throughput requirements if you over-warm.
[01:36] Maya: so are you precomputing full KV for the whole prompt or just key blocks? our prompts are large, like 1.2k tokens.
[01:43] Luis: we do selective KV for the prefix segments, typically compressing or quantizing, and we allow TTLs per entry. For giant prompts we recommend splitting system + history so the system instructions remain hot.
[01:55] [01:58] Jordan: quick interjection — i want to show a simulated cost model. switching to the cost tab.
[02:05] Jordan: here's a baseline: no prefix cache, batching size 1, average request length 350 tokens. monthly QPS ~ 20 RPS peak, sustained 8 RPS. Estimated monthly token charges and GPU unit time show $41k.
[02:22] Alex: whoa, that's above our threshold. how much can prefetch help?
[02:26] Priya: depends on hit rate. if you get a 60% prefix hit on system+template tokens and use small batching (batch of 4 with 30 ms batching window), our sim shows cost drop to ~ $19k with p95 latency at ~82 ms.
[02:40] Samir: 82 ms p95 is okay, but our SLA is 75 ms — is there a configuration to tighten latency while preserving cost?
[02:48] Priya: yes. two levers: reduce the batching window (down to 10-15 ms) and enable session-affinity routing so hot sessions hit the same worker and avoid cross-worker KV fetch. that pushes p95 down to about 68 ms but increases cost to ~ $23k in the sim.
[03:07] Maya: where is the break-even point between hosted and dedicated for us? We're currently on cloud VMs.
[03:12] Jordan: great question, quick rule of thumb — for steady sustained throughput with tight latency SLOs, Dedicated reserved capacity pays off once you exceed ~ 15-20 RPS sustained for large models; console has a dedicated estimator that models reserved GPU amortization. for your numbers (sustained 8 RPS) hosted with optimize batching/prefetch might be cheaper for now.
[03:30] Alex: makes sense. can you show the specific recommendation tile?
[03:34] Priya: sure pulling up a recommendation: "Enable prefix cache (TTL 30m), prefetch top N-templates (N=5) for new session, batching window 20ms, target batch size 4, session affinity enabled." It also shows expected hit rate 48-64% depending on template variance.
[03:54] Jordan: note the console includes a sensitivity slider — you can bias towards latency or cost and it recalculates suggestions in real time.
[04:05] [04:07] Alex: that sensitivity slider is useful. how accurate are your hit rate estimates? we have a lot of long-tail prompts.
[04:12] Priya: accuracy is proportional to your sample trace representativeness. we use your anonymized traces to compute prefix frequency and a simulated hit-rate model, but for  long-tail heavy apps we instrument a smaller TTL and tune N. also you can run a sandbox sim — Luis, can you show the sandbox?
[04:29] Luis: yep — sandbox sim run; uploading a small sample trace now. (file: novaforge_sample_24h.json) — note: we keep it anonymized. running a 6-hour sim to estimate hit rates and batching distributions.
[04:45] Maya: quick question — our session tokens include user-specific signals, does that kill cache effectiveness?
[04:50] Priya: if templates contain user-specific tokens, we recommend template extraction: normalize variable portions (IDs, names) so they don't poison the prefix index. we have heuristics and a small SDK helper to do that extraction.
[05:02] Samir: regarding security — we need to ensure prefetch doesn't persist PII in cache. what's redwood's approach?
[05:08] Jordan: good callout. cache entries can be encrypted at rest with customer-managed keys (KMS) in Private deployments. For hosted we offer strict TTLs, automatic PII redaction hooks, and audit logs. we'll send SOC2 / encryption docs after the call.
[05:23] Alex: perfect. some of our compliance folks will want explicit proof of KMS integration.
[05:27] Jordan: noted — action item for me to include the KMS note in the package.
[05:31] [05:33] Priya: sandbox results are in — rough numbers: prefix hit 52%, average batch size 3.1 with a 20ms window, estimated monthly cost $21k with p95 79 ms. i'm going to open the sensitivity analysis to show a fast path.
[05:47] Priya: slider -> bias latency, reduce window to 12 ms, session affinity on; new estimate: hit rate drops slightly to 49% but p95 66 ms and monthly cost $24k.
[06:00] Maya: that matches our intuition, lower latency costs more. question — how does quantized kernels/compilation interact with KV cache? we do 4-bit quant for cheaper compute.
[06:09] Luis: runtime supports quantized execution; kv cache entries are format agnostic — we'll rehydrate compressed KV into the execution path. quantization tends to reduce GPU time per token but cache miss penalty is still there; you get best of both worlds with high hit rates.
[06:26] Samir: do you support adaptive batching? e.g., increase batch size under high load but keep low window for low-latency paths.
[06:33] Priya: yes — the console can define adaptive policies: minimum window 10 ms for latency-sensitive routes and up to 60 ms when CPU/GPU utilization low, with a trigger on queue length. we often recommend an aggressive cold-start policy for spiky loads.
[06:47] Alex: what about multi-model routing? sometimes we route to a smaller distilled model for short prompts.
[06:52] Jordan: console supports model routing by policy (latency, cost, quality). you can set a decision tree: if token count < 80 and confidence threshold met, route to tiny model; else large model. this pairs well with prefix cache because small-model calls avoid expensive KV ops.
[07:07] Maya: i saw a note about "prefix eviction heuristics" — is that LRU?
[07:11] Luis: it's LRU + frequency weighting; we also have TTLs and a manual pin list for critical templates.
[07:19] [07:20] Alex: are there pitfalls we should watch out for during rollout? any gotchas?
[07:24] Priya: two main gotchas: 1) over-aggressive prefetching that warms too many prefixes and increases overall token throughput; 2) templates with embedded user IDs that reduce hit rate — both are mitigated by our preflight sim and template extraction tool.
[07:39] Jordan: also monitor the Console's quality regression alert; if prefix caching changes outputs for generation quality-sensitive apps, we flag it.
[07:45] Maya: how do you validate quality differences? we have a hundred-shot eval set.
[07:49] Priya: we run prompt-level regressions using your eval set in the console – if scores drop beyond your tolerance we trigger a rollback or route to a different model variant.
[07:59] Samir: On the billing side, how granular is the cost reporting? we want per-route token-level breakdown.
[08:05] Jordan: Console provides token-level breakdown per model & route, plus cost per prefix and cost allocated to prefetch warms. you can export CSV to feed into your finance system.
[08:17] Alex: sweet. can you attach an example export?
[08:19] Jordan: yes will send with the spreadsheet.
[08:21] [08:24] Maya: can we talk about TTL sizing — 30m seems long for us, maybe 5m is safer for privacy.
[08:29] Priya: TTL is a knob; in sandbox we can run TTL sweeps, e.g., 5m/15m/30m and show hit rate vs cost curves. shorter TTL reduces privacy exposure but lowers hit rate and increases cost.
[08:45] Alex: operational question: if we do a POC, what support do you provide? SE-led bench?
[08:50] Luis: yes, POC includes SE bench runs, a dedicated sandbox for your traces, and a runbook for rollout. we can scope a 2-week POC.
[08:59] Alex: timeline-wise our procurement window is mid-August, so a POC in the next 2 weeks would be ideal.
[09:06] Jordan: we can start a POC week-of-2028-07-31. Priya, Luis — does that align with your bandwidth?
[09:12] Priya: yes, we can allocate time.
[09:14] [09:16] Jordan: ok next i'll quickly demo the cost-sensitivity toggles. switching back to the estimate view, here we can toggle "aggressive prefetch" vs "conservative prefetch" and plot cost vs latency bands.
[09:28] Jordan: for conservative prefetch + batch size 2, monthly cost estimated $26k and p95 at 72 ms.
[09:35] Alex: that's within our budget if optimized further. can we map to our $25k target? maybe reduce model size for short queries and keep prefetch for long ones.
[09:44] Priya: exactly — hybrid model routing + prefix cache for long prompts is a common pattern to shave costs.
[09:50] Maya: anything specific about GPU types? we currently use A100s in our own infra.
[09:54] Luis: Redwood runtime chooses kernels per hardware; A100 vs H100 tradeoffs are modeled. for prefetch heavy workloads H100 can be more throughput-efficient per dollar in some clouds; console can model per-region pricing.
[10:08] Samir: we need to ensure networking between our VPC and private deployment is secure — port requirements?
[10:14] Jordan: for Private we provide a control-plane VPN and you can use peered VPC endpoints; we'll share a network setup doc.
[10:21] Alex: excellent.
[10:25] [10:27] Priya: quick demo of the runbook generator — when you apply recommendations the console auto-generates an ops runbook listing configuration changes, rollout steps, and monitoring checks. it's handy for SRE/DevOps.
[10:42] Tasha: can the runbook be exported as Confluence or an RFC?
[10:46] Priya: yes exports to Markdown, Confluence, and a Jira ticket template.
[10:51] Alex: ok any final technical risks?
[10:54] Priya: aside from privacy/TTL and over-prefetching, the other risk is mismatching the sample trace — if the trace is not representative the sim will give optimistic hit rates. make sure to include weekend/peak patterns.
[11:08] Jordan: we should recap next steps. Jordan to send cost spreadsheet, SOC2/KMS docs. Priya to run a more complete sim on the traces Alex will provide. schedule POC for week of 2028-07-31.
[11:21] Alex: i'll share traces and some of our top prompt templates by end of week.
[11:25] Maya: and i'll outline our eval set so we can run quality checks.
[11:30] Samir: i'll be on the POC call for infra.
[11:33] Jordan: great, thanks everyone. any last questions?
[11:36] Alex: none from me. thank you.
[11:38] Jordan: cool, we'll follow up with the materials. bye!
